title: Types
text:
Inference
phibble infers a column’s type from its PHP values the way R’s c() combines values:

Bools and ints combine to int, and ints and floats combine to float.
Any string makes the column a string column, and the other values are converted to text.
DateTimeInterface values make a datetime column, and Phibble\Time values make a time column.
Arrays and other objects make a list-column.
A column that is entirely NA is bool, R’s logical type.

$df = DataFrame::fromColumns([
    'logical' => [true, false, null],
    'whole' => [1, 2, null],
    'mixed' => [1, 2.5, null],
    'with_bool' => [true, 2, 3],
    'text' => ['a', 1, null],
    'when' => [
        new DateTimeImmutable('2024-03-01 09:30'),
        null,
        null,
    ],
    'nested' => [[1, 2], [3], null],
    'empty' => [null, null, null],
]);

echo $df->glimpse();
Rows: 3
Columns: 8
$ logical   <lgl> TRUE, FALSE, NA
$ whole     <int> 1, 2, NA
$ mixed     <dbl> 1.0, 2.5, NA
$ with_bool <int> 1, 2, 3
$ text      <chr> "a", "1", NA
$ when      <dttm> 2024-03-01 09:30:00, NA, NA
$ nested    <list> <1, 2>, 3, <NULL>
$ empty     <lgl> NA, NA, NA
Text read from CSV files and databases is guessed differently. The input and output guide describes that.

title: Types
text:
Factors
A factor column stores an ordered list of level labels and one code per row. asFactor() sorts the unique values to make the levels unless levels are given. Numbers sort numerically and text sorts in byte order. Values that are not among explicit levels become NA.
levels() returns the labels. storage('x')->codes() returns the codes, which are 0-based indexes into the levels. An ordered factor sorts by level position.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/'
        .'main/csv/penguins.csv'
)->asFactor('species');

echo json_encode($penguins->levels('species')), "\n";
$codes = $penguins->storage('species')->codes();
echo json_encode(array_slice($codes, 150, 5)), "\n";

$sizes = tibble(size: ['small', 'large', 'medium', 'small'])
    ->asOrdered('size', ['small', 'medium', 'large']);

echo $sizes->arrange(['size']), "\n";
var_dump($sizes->isOrdered('size'));
["Adelie","Chinstrap","Gentoo"]
[0,0,2,2,2]
# A tibble: 4 × 1
  size  
  <ord> 
1 small 
2 small 
3 medium
4 large 
bool(true)
The forcats functions are fct* methods. Each returns a new data frame with the column’s levels changed.







Method
Effect




fctRelevel($col, $levels, after: 0)
Moves the given levels to the front, or after a position.


fctLevels($col, $levels)
Sets the full level order.


fctRev($col)
Reverses the level order.


fctInorder($col)
Orders levels by first appearance.


fctInfreq($col)
Orders levels by frequency, most common first.


fctReorder($col, $by, $summary)
Orders levels by a summary of another column, the median by default.


fctRecode($col, ['new' => 'old'])
Renames levels.


fctCollapse($col, ['new' => ['a', 'b']])
Merges levels.


fctDrop($col)
Removes levels that no row uses.



$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/'
        .'main/csv/penguins.csv'
)->asFactor('species');

$mean = fn ($xs) => array_sum(array_filter($xs))
    / count(array_filter($xs));

$versions = [
    'sorted (default)' => $penguins,
    'fctRelevel Gentoo' => $penguins
        ->fctRelevel('species', ['Gentoo']),
    'fctInfreq' => $penguins->fctInfreq('species'),
    'fctReorder by body_mass_g' => $penguins
        ->fctReorder('species', 'body_mass_g', $mean),
    'fctRev' => $penguins->fctRev('species'),
    'fctRecode' => $penguins
        ->fctRecode('species', ['Chinstrap penguin' => 'Chinstrap']),
    'fctCollapse' => $penguins
        ->fctCollapse('species', ['brush-tailed' => ['Adelie', 'Gentoo']]),
];

foreach ($versions as $label => $f) {
    echo \str_pad($label, 26), json_encode($f->levels('species')), "\n";
}

fctRelevel Gentoo         ["Gentoo","Adelie","Chinstrap"]
fctInfreq                 ["Adelie","Gentoo","Chinstrap"]
fctReorder by body_mass_g ["Adelie","Chinstrap","Gentoo"]
fctRev                    ["Gentoo","Chinstrap","Adelie"]
fctRecode                 ["Adelie","Chinstrap penguin","Gentoo"]

title: Types
text:
Dates and datetimes
A date column holds DateTimeImmutable values at midnight UTC. A datetime column holds DateTimeImmutable values with their time and time zone. CSV text in ISO 8601 form is parsed as a date when it has no time, and as a datetime otherwise. Text without an offset is read as UTC.
$visits = DataFrame::fromCsvString(<<<'CSV'
    day,checked_in
    2024-01-02,2024-01-02T09:15:00Z
    2024-01-03,2024-01-03 14:40:00
    CSV);

echo $visits, "\n";
echo $visits->cast(['day' => 'float', 'checked_in' => 'float']);
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  day        checked_in         
  <date>     <dttm>             
1 2024-01-02 2024-01-02 09:15:00
2 2024-01-03 2024-01-03 14:40:00
# A tibble: 2 × 2
    day checked_in
  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 19724 1704186900
2 19725 1704292800

title: Types
text:
Times
A time column holds Phibble\Time values, as R’s hms package does. A time is a whole number of microseconds, which may be negative or longer than a day. Time::of($hours, $minutes, $seconds) and Time::fromSeconds() build one, and Time::parse() reads text such as 07:30, -01:00:00.5, or 1:30 PM. seconds() gives the number of seconds. hour(), minute(), and second() give the clock time, as lubridate does, so 25:00:00 has hour 1.
A time column prints as hms prints it. It shows seconds only when a value has them, the fraction digits the column needs, and MM'SS" when no value has hours. Casts lists its conversions.
$trains = DataFrame::fromCsvString(<<<'CSV'
    train,departs
    A,7:05 AM
    B,12:40 PM
    C,6:15 PM
    D,NA
    CSV);

echo $trains, "\n";

echo $trains
    ->filter(col('departs')->gt('12:00'))
    ->mutate([
        'hour' => hour(col('departs')),
        'later' => col('departs')->add(90 * 60),
    ]), "\n";

echo Time::of(1, 30), "\n";
echo Time::fromSeconds(-90.5), "\n";
echo Time::parse('25:00')?->seconds(), "\n";
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  train departs
  <chr> <time> 
1 A     07:05  
2 B     12:40  
3 C     18:15  
4 D        NA  
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  train departs  hour later 
  <chr> <time>  <int> <time>
1 B     12:40      12 14:10 
2 C     18:15      18 19:45 
01:30:00
-00:01:30.5
90000
Comparing a time with text reads the text as a time, so col('departs')->gt('12:00') compares clock times. Adding or subtracting seconds or a time gives a time, and so does multiplying or dividing by a number.

text:
Queries that stay in the database
use function Phibble\Expr\{col, mean, n};

$summary = Penguin::query()
    ->measured()
    ->where('year', '>=', 2008)
    ->phibble()
    ->groupBy(['species', 'sex'])
    ->summarize([
        'n' => n(),
        'mass' => mean(col('body_mass_g')),
    ]);

echo $summary->collect();
# A tibble: 7 × 4
# Groups:   species [3]
  species   sex        n  mass
  <chr>     <chr>  <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie    female    51 3360.
2 Adelie    male      51 4046.
3 Chinstrap female    21 3501.
4 Chinstrap male      21 4013.
5 Gentoo    female    42 4703.
6 Gentoo    male      44 5459.
7 Gentoo    <NA>       3 4750

The builder’s SQL, bindings, and scopes become the table’s source, and phibble’s methods add to that query.
Nothing runs until the rows are needed, as with collect(), printing, or nrow().
Global scopes such as SoftDeletes apply. Attribute casts and accessors do not, because the rows come from SQL.

This grouped filter keeps the heaviest penguin on each island.
use function Phibble\Expr\{col, max};

$heaviest = Penguin::query()
    ->measured()
    ->phibble()
    ->groupBy(['island'])
    ->filter(col('body_mass_g')->eq(max(col('body_mass_g'))))
    ->select(['island', 'species', 'body_mass_g']);

echo $heaviest->showQuery(), "\n\n";
echo $heaviest->arrange(['island'])->collect();

SELECT "island", "species", "body_mass_g" FROM (SELECT "island", "species", "body_mass_g", "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT "id", "species", "island", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g", "sex", "year", "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT *, ("body_mass_g" = (CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY "island") > COUNT("body_mass_g") OVER (PARTITION BY "island") THEN NULL ELSE (CASE WHEN COUNT("body_mass_g") OVER (PARTITION BY "island") = 0 THEN -9e999 ELSE MAX("body_mass_g") OVER (PARTITION BY "island") END) END)) AS "__phibble_keep" FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS "__phibble_row" FROM (select * from "penguins" where "body_mass_g" is not null) AS phibble_source) AS q1) AS q2 WHERE "__phibble_keep" = TRUE) AS q3) AS q4 ORDER BY ("__phibble_row" IS NULL), "__phibble_row"

title: Expressions
text:
Build column computations with col() and the functions in Phibble\Expr, and pass them to table methods. An expression runs on every backend: DataFrame evaluates it, SqlTable compiles it to SQL, and PolarsTable maps it to Polars. Each backend follows R’s semantics and runs a function in memory when it has no exact translation. Results can still differ where a database cannot represent R’s value, as SQL tables lists.
Table methods also accept PHP closures. A closure can only run in PHP, so a SQL or Polars table loads its rows to run one.

title: Expressions
text:
Using expressions with table methods
Each method evaluates expressions per group:

filter() keeps rows where the expression is true. NA counts as false.
mutate() adds a column with one value per row. An aggregate such as mean() gives one value per group, which is repeated for each row of the group.
summarize() needs one value per group. Anything else throws a LengthException.
arrange() sorts by expressions over the whole table, ignoring groups. Wrap a key in desc() to sort it in descending order.

$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/'
        .'main/csv/penguins.csv'
);

$out = $penguins
    ->filter(is_na(col('body_mass_g'))->not())
    ->groupBy(['species'])
    ->mutate([
        'z' => col('body_mass_g')
            ->sub(mean(col('body_mass_g')))
            ->div(sd(col('body_mass_g'))),
        'rank' => min_rank(desc(col('body_mass_g'))),
        'size' => case_when(
            col('body_mass_g')->ge(5000), 'large',
            col('body_mass_g')->ge(3500), 'medium',
            default: 'small',
        ),
    ])
    ->filter(col('rank')->le(2))
    ->select(['species', 'body_mass_g', 'z', 'rank', 'size']);

text:
Functions

Scalar functions
Scalar functions return one value per row.







Function
Notes




is_na(x)
True for NA and NaN.


if_else(cond, true, false, missing:)
missing is used where cond is NA.


case_when(c1, v1, c2, v2, ..., default:)
The first true condition wins. NA conditions count as false.


coalesce(x, y, ...)
The first non-NA value.


x->isIn([...])
Never NA. NA is in the set only if NA is listed.


between(x, low, high)
Inclusive. NA if any argument is NA.


na_if(x, y)
NA where x == y.


near(x, y, tol:)
Equality within a tolerance.


abs, sqrt, exp, log(x, base:), log10, floor, ceiling
Math functions.


round(x, digits:)
Rounds as R 4 does.


as_int, as_float, as_string, as_bool
Casts with R’s as.*() rules.


paste0(...), paste(..., sep:)
NA becomes the text NA, as in R.





Text functions (stringr)
As in stringr, a pattern given as text is a regular expression. phibble uses PCRE and matches by Unicode character; stringr uses ICU, and the two agree on common patterns. fixed('...') matches the text literally, and regex('...', ignore_case: true) sets options.







Function
Notes




str_detect, str_starts, str_ends (with negate:)
str_starts and str_ends anchor the pattern.


str_count(x, pattern)
Non-overlapping matches.


str_extract(x, pattern)
The first match, or NA.


str_extract_all(x, pattern), str_split(x, pattern)
A list-column. NA gives a list holding NA.


str_split_i(x, pattern, i)
The i-th piece; negative i counts from the end; NA when out of range.


str_replace, str_replace_all
\1 in the replacement refers to a group. An NA replacement gives NA where the pattern matches.


str_pad(x, width, side:, pad:)
side is left (default), right, or both.


str_trunc(x, width, side:, ellipsis:)
side is right (default), left, or center.


str_to_upper, str_to_lower, str_to_title, str_squish
Title case capitalizes after a hyphen but not after an apostrophe, as ICU does.


str_length, str_trim(x, side:), str_sub(x, start, end)
str_sub is 1-based and inclusive; negative positions count from the end.


str_lower, str_upper
Aliases of str_to_lower and str_to_upper.





Dates and times (lubridate)
Date functions accept dates and datetimes, and a date stays a date: results such as floor_date(d, 'month') or d + days(1) are dates when d is.







Function
Notes




ymd, dmy, mdy, ymd_hms, dmy_hms, mdy_hms (with tz:)
Parse text. Separators are optional; invalid input gives NA.


parse_date_time(x, orders, tz:)
Orders made of Y, y, m, d, H, M, and S, such as 'Ymd HMS'; the first that fits wins.


year, month, day, yday, quarter, hour, minute, second
Parts as numbers. On a time, hour(), minute(), and second() give its clock time, and the date parts throw.


wday(x, week_start:)
1 is Sunday by default, as in lubridate; week_start: 1 makes Monday 1.


floor_date, ceiling_date, round_date (x, unit, week_start:)
Units from second to year, with multiples such as '15 minutes'. ceiling_date moves a date that is already on a boundary to the next one, as lubridate does for dates.


seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years
Periods, used as col('d')->add(months(1)). Month and year arithmetic that lands on a date that does not exist gives NA.


difftime(x, y, units:)
A number in secs, mins, hours, days (default), or weeks. date - date gives days and datetime - datetime seconds.


with_tz(x, tz), force_tz(x, tz)
The same instant in another zone; the same clock time in another zone (NA for a time the zone skips).


today(tz:), now(tz:)
Read Phibble\Expr\Clock, which tests can freeze.





Aggregates
An aggregate returns one value per group. Each takes na_rm:, which is false by default, so an aggregate over a group containing NA returns NA unless na_rm: true.







Function
Notes




n()
Rows in the group.


sum, mean, median, min, max
sum of no values is 0 and mean is NaN.


sd, var_
Sample statistics, with n - 1.


quantile(x, p), iqr(x)
R’s default type 7. These throw on NA unless na_rm: true, as R does.

title: Expressions
text:
NA and arithmetic
Expressions follow R’s rules for missing values and arithmetic:

Arithmetic and comparisons with NA give NA.
& and | use three-valued logic. FALSE & NA is false and TRUE | NA is true.
/ and ^ always return floats. Division by zero gives Inf, -Inf, or NaN.
%% takes the sign of the divisor, so -7 %% 3 is 2.
round() takes, of the two candidates, the one closer to the stored value, and an exact tie goes to the even digit. round(2.5) is 2, and round(2.675, digits: 2) is 2.67 because 2.675 is stored as slightly less than 2.675.
Text compares and sorts in byte order.

$df = tibble(
    a: [true, false, null, null],
    b: [null, null, true, false],
    x: [2.5, 0.5, -1.5, 2.675],
    y: [1, null, 3, 4],
);

echo $df->mutate([
    'and' => col('a')->and(col('b')),
    'or' => col('a')->or(col('b')),
    'sum' => col('y')->add(1),
    'round' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x')),
    'round2' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x'), digits: 2),
    'mod' => lit(-7)->mod(3),
    'cumsum' => cumsum(col('y')),
]);

title: Expressions
Query a database table
The Table contract
text: Phibble\Contracts\Table is the interface that every table backend implements: DataFrame, Phibble\Sql\SqlTable, and Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable. phplyr’s functions call its methods, so a pipeline runs unchanged on any backend. This page lists the rules every implementation follows and the semantics of each method.

title: The Table contract
text:
Rules

Immutability. Every method returns a new table and leaves the original unchanged.
Return types. Methods are declared to return Table. A backend may return a different implementation. SqlTable returns a DataFrame when it falls back to memory for a closure. DataFrame declares static.
NA. PHP null is NA in every column type.
Grouping. groupBy() records grouping columns as metadata. filter(), mutate(), mutateGroups(), filterGroups(), summarise(), and eachGroup() work per group. The other methods keep the grouping.
Group order. Groups are visited in sorted key order, as in dplyr: ascending, factors by level order, NA last, and strings in byte order.
Row order. filter() and mutate() keep the rows in their input order. arrange() sorts stably, so rows with equal keys keep their input order. A SqlTable’s input order is the order in which the database returns the source query’s rows, which a stored table does not fix. See Row order and window functions.
Rowwise tables. rowwise() makes every row its own group, in row order. groups() returns its id columns.
Row closures. A row closure receives (Phibble\Row $row, Table $group). $group is the row’s group, or the whole table when ungrouped.
Expressions. Wherever a method accepts a closure, it also accepts a Phibble\Expr\Expr, evaluated per group with the semantics in the expression reference.
Errors. An unknown column name throws Phibble\Exception\ColumnNotFound.
Countable and iterable. count() equals nrow(), and iterating yields one Phibble\Row per row.

title: The Table contract
text:
Methods

Shape and data







Method
Returns




columns()
Column names in order.

Column name to Phibble\Type.


nrow(), ncol()
Row and column counts.


column($name)
One column as a list. Factors return their labels.

A list of associative arrays.

An array of lists by column name.

The rows as an in-memory DataFrame. A DataFrame returns itself.





Methods







Method
Semantics




select($names)
Keeps the named columns in the given order. Grouping columns are always kept.


filter($predicate)
Keeps rows where the closure or expression is true. NA counts as false.


filterGroups($fn)
Runs $fn once per group with the group’s table. It returns one value per row, and truthy values keep the row.


mutate($columns)
Adds or replaces columns. A value is a row closure, an expression, a list with one value per row, or a scalar. Later entries see earlier ones. Replaced columns keep their position.


mutateGroups($columns)
Like mutate(), but a closure runs once per group and returns a list for the group’s rows or a scalar. This is the primitive for window functions.


rename($map)
Renames columns, with new => old entries as in dplyr.


arrange($keys)
Sorts stably. Keys are names, [name, 'asc'|'desc'] pairs, or expressions, and NA sorts last in both directions. It ignores grouping.


groupBy($names), ungroup(), groups()
Set, clear, or read the grouping columns.


groupBy($names, drop: false), dropsEmptyGroups()
dplyr’s .drop = FALSE: grouped operations also visit empty groups. A factor key yields every level; a non-factor key yields its observed values, or NA under an empty group. Row verbs keep the flag; groupBy() and ungroup() reset it.


rowwise($idColumns), isRowwise()
Set or read rowwise mode. groupBy() and ungroup() clear it.


eachGroup()
Yields ['key' => [...], 'table' => Table] for each group, with ungrouped tables. An ungrouped table yields one group with an empty key.


groupRows()
Returns ['key' => [...], 'rows' => [...]] for each group, in eachGroup() order, with the group’s 0-based row positions. Empty groups have no rows, and a rowwise table has one group per row.


summarise($aggregates)
DataFrame, SqlTable, and PolarsTable also have the alias summarize(), which the interface does not declare. Returns one row per group: the keys, then one column per entry. Each entry is a closure given the group’s table or an expression of size 1. The result drops the last grouping level, and a rowwise table keeps its id columns. The optional second argument is dplyr’s .groups: 'drop_last' (the default), 'drop', 'keep', or 'rowwise'.


distinct($names)
Keeps the first row of each combination of the named columns (and the grouping columns), and only those columns. An empty list means all columns.


pivotLongerSpec($spec, dropNa:)
tidyr’s pivot_longer_spec(). Spec rows are ['.name' => source, '.value' => value column, ...name parts]. Output: id columns, name parts, then one column per .value; each input row yields one row per name-part combination in spec order. Values combine by vctrs rules.


pivotWiderSpec($spec, idColumns:, valuesFill:)
tidyr’s pivot_wider_spec(). Spec rows are ['.name' => new column, '.value' => values column, ...names_from values]. New columns follow spec order; rows follow the first appearance of each id combination. Duplicates make every new column a list-column and raise tidyr’s warning.


take($indices)
Rows by 0-based position, in the given order. A null index gives an all-NA row. Keeps types, factor levels, and grouping.


slice($offset, $length), head($n)
Rows by position. These ignore grouping.


join($other, $by, $type, ...)
Joins with dplyr 1.1 semantics, described below.





Joins
join() takes the other table, a list of conditions, and the join type: inner, left, right, full, semi, anti, or cross. A cross join takes no conditions. The conditions follow dplyr’s join_by(), and all of them must hold:

'k', [$l, $r], or $l => $r: equality.
[$l, $op, $r] with $op in ==, >=, >, <=, or <: a comparison.
['closest', $l, $op, $r], at most one per join: of the y rows that satisfy the other conditions and the comparison, keep only those with the largest $r (for >= and >) or the smallest (for <= and <). Ties keep every tied row.

dplyr’s between(), within(), and overlaps() are expressed as pairs of comparisons.

Columns. The result has x’s columns, then y’s columns. Clashing names get the suffixes, .x and .y by default.
Keys. keep is null by default. Equality keys then come from x only, and for rows that only y has (right and full joins) they are filled from y’s keys. Columns used in comparisons are kept from both tables. With keep: true every key column is kept from both tables. keep: false throws when a comparison or closest condition is present, as in dplyr.
Rows. Rows follow x’s order, and each x row’s matches follow y’s order. Right and full joins then add y’s unmatched rows in y’s order. Semi and anti joins keep x’s rows and columns and never duplicate rows.
Matching. NA keys match each other unless naMatches: false. In a comparison, NA against NA satisfies >= and <= but not > or <, and NA never matches a value. 1 matches 1.0, and a factor matches text by its label.
Options. multiple picks all, any, first, or last match per x row. relationship (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many) throws when the data violates it. Without it, an unexpected many-to-many equality join raises a warning, as dplyr does. unmatched: 'error' throws when the join would drop rows.
Grouping. The result keeps x’s grouping.

title: The Table contract
text:
Errors and allowed differences
DataFrame follows R, and other backends match it. The following rules apply where R raises an error or where exact agreement is impractical.

quantile() and iqr() over values that include NA, without na_rm: true, throw an error, as R does. A backend must not return NA.
A summary entry that is not size 1 throws LengthException, and the message mentions reframe().
Aggregates over zero rows may return NA. DataFrame returns R’s values (NaN for mean(), Inf and -Inf for min() and max()). This case only arises for an ungrouped table with no rows.
as_string() on doubles with very large or very small magnitudes may differ from R’s scientific notation. Phibble\Column\Infer::formatFloat() states R’s rule: 15 significant digits, in fixed or scientific notation, whichever is shorter.

title: The Table contract
text:
Testing a backend
The simplest test of a backend is to run the same operations on the backend and on DataFrame and compare the results. tests/SqlTest.php does this for SqlTable. It loads the same data into a database, runs each operation both ways, and compares the collected rows. It also runs every case in tests/fixtures/expr/expected.json, the dplyr results that tests/r/expr.R produces, so each backend is checked against R as well as against DataFrame.

title: Backends
text:
Run the same pipeline in memory, in a database, or in Polars. Every table method is part of the Phibble\Contracts\Table interface, and three classes implement it:
Code written against Table, including phplyr’s functions, runs on any of them. A backend that cannot run a step exactly, such as a PHP closure or a function with no exact translation, loads its rows into PHP and runs the step in a DataFrame. Later steps also run in memory. Results match DataFrame with these exceptions:
The Table contract page states the rules each backend follows.

title: Backends
Backends
text:
The Polars backend
PolarsTable loads only when used, so phibble runs without the extension.

Expressions, joins (including join_by comparisons and rolling joins), pivots, and the lubridate and stringr functions run in Polars.
Steps it cannot run, such as PHP closures and str_to_title(), run in a DataFrame. PolarsTable::$fallbacks counts them.
PolarsTable::$strict = true throws PolarsFallback instead, naming the method and the reason.

Type mapping:

A time column is a Polars duration in microseconds, which, like an hms, can be negative or longer than a day. A Polars Time column reads as a time.
Comparisons of times, is_na(), min(), max(), first(), and last() run in Polars. Other functions of a time run in a DataFrame, as do sum(), mean(), median(), quantile(), sd(), var(), and iqr() of dates and datetimes.
fromTable() throws on a list-column of named arrays with different keys, since Polars structs have every key in every row, and on a list-column of DataFrames.

The Polars test suite runs phibble’s dplyr, tidyr, lubridate, and stringr reference cases on PolarsTable and skips when the extension is not loaded.

title: Coming from tibble
text:
Differences
phibble differs from R in these places:

Whole numbers guess as int. readr guesses 1,2,3 as double. phibble guesses int, which suits PHP. Pass types: 'd' to read a double.
Positions are 0-based. addRow(before:), addColumn(before:), take(), slice(), and row() count rows and columns from 0.
Regular expressions are PCRE. As in stringr, a text pattern is a regular expression and fixed() matches literally. phibble uses PCRE where stringr uses ICU. SqlTable runs most regular-expression patterns in memory, as the SQL tables page lists.
Times are Phibble\Time values in whole microseconds. hms stores seconds as a double. The mean(), sum(), min(), and max() of a time column are times, where dplyr gives a difftime. The mean and median of a date are whole days, where R keeps a fraction of a day.
JSON keeps null values. jsonlite drops NA fields from records. toJson() writes them as null.
Datetimes are UTC. Text without an offset is read as UTC, and text with an offset is converted to UTC, as readr does.
Strings sort in byte order. Sorting, grouping, and factor levels use the C locale, as dplyr’s arrange() does. Base R’s factor() uses the system locale, which can order mixed-case levels differently.
Packed data frame columns are not supported. An unnamed table in tibble() is spliced into columns. A named one throws.

Load
DataFrame::fromCsv() reads a CSV file, or a URL, and guesses each column’s type. Here it reads the Palmer penguins data, whose rownames column holds the row numbers the table had in R. Reading and writing data covers the options, JSON, and databases.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/'
        .'main/csv/penguins.csv'
);

echo $penguins;

tibble() builds a data frame column by column:

A list gives one value per row, and a single value is repeated.
A closure receives the columns built so far.

These values are the first four penguins in the data:
$penguins = tibble(
    species: 'Adelie',
    island: ['Torgersen', 'Torgersen', 'Torgersen', 'Torgersen'],
    body_mass_g: [3750, 3800, 3250, null],
    heavy: fn (DataFrame $t) => array_map(
        fn ($m) => $m === null ? null : $m >= 3500,
        $t['body_mass_g'],
    ),
);

echo $penguins;
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  species island    body_mass_g heavy
  <chr>   <chr>           <int> <lgl>
1 Adelie  Torgersen        3750 TRUE 
2 Adelie  Torgersen        3800 TRUE 
3 Adelie  Torgersen        3250 FALSE
4 Adelie  Torgersen          NA NA
tribble() takes the column names first, then one list per row. These are the three New York City airports from nycflights13:
$airports = tribble(
    ['faa', 'name', 'lat', 'lon'],
    ['EWR', 'Newark Liberty Intl', 40.6925, -74.168667],
    ['JFK', 'John F Kennedy Intl', 40.639751, -73.778925],

$rows = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['species' => 'Adelie', 'island' => 'Torgersen', 'body_mass_g' => 3750],
    ['species' => 'Adelie', 'island' => 'Torgersen'],
]);

Summarize
groupBy() records grouping columns, and summarize() (or summarise()) returns one row per group:

Groups are sorted, with NA last, as in dplyr.
With several grouping columns, the result keeps all but the last.
In a grouped data frame, filter() and mutate() work within each group, and an aggregate in mutate() repeats for each row of its group.
A row closure receives the row’s group as its second argument: fn (Row $r, DataFrame $group) => ....

$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/'
        .'main/csv/penguins.csv'
)
    ->dropNa(['body_mass_g']);

$centered = $penguins
    ->groupBy(['species'])
    ->mutate([
        'vs_species' => col('body_mass_g')
            ->sub(mean(col('body_mass_g'))),
    ])
    ->select(['species', 'body_mass_g', 'vs_species'])
    ->head(4);

echo $centered;
# A tibble: 4 × 3
# Groups:   species [1]
  species body_mass_g vs_species

1 Adelie         3750       49.3
2 Adelie         3800       99.3

    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/'
        .'main/csv/penguins.csv'
)
    ->asFactor('species')
    ->filter(col('species')->ne('Chinstrap'));

    ->groupBy(['species'], drop: false)
    ->summarize(['n' => n()]);

title: Reading and writing data
text:
CSV files
DataFrame::fromCsv() reads delimited text the way readr’s read_csv() and read_delim() do. DataFrame::fromCsvString() reads from a string. fromCsv() takes:

a path, decompressing files that end in .gz,
an http:// or https:// URL, which needs PHP’s allow_url_fopen. The file is downloaded to a temporary file, read, and deleted, and a failed download throws with the URL and the reason,
an open stream.

$url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets'
    .'/main/csv/mroz.csv';
$mroz = DataFrame::fromCsv($url);

Options
readr’s options are named arguments in camelCase:








Option
Default
Meaning

guess
Column types, as a compact string or by name.


delimiter
','
The field separator.


na
['', 'NA']
Text that is read as NA.

true
true reads a header row, false names columns X1, X2, and so on, and a list gives the names.

all
Columns to keep, in this order.


skip
0
Lines to skip before the header.


nMax
all
The most rows to read.


comment
''
Lines starting with this text are skipped.


quote
'"'
The quoting character.


trimWs
true
Trim spaces around unquoted values.


skipEmptyRows

Skip blank lines.

1000

decimalMark, groupingMark

$text = <<<'CSV'
    # exported 2024-06-01
    id;zip;score;visited
    1;02134;3,5;2024-05-01
    2;10001;-;2024-05-03
    3;94110;4,25;2024-05-04
    CSV;

$df = DataFrame::fromCsvString(
    $text,
    types: ['zip' => 'c'],
    delimiter: ';',
    na: ['-'],
    comment: '#',
    decimalMark: ',',
);

echo $df;
# A tibble: 3 × 4
     id zip   score visited   
  <int> <chr> <dbl> <date>    
1     1 02134  3.5  2024-05-01
2     2 10001 NA    2024-05-03
3     3 94110  4.25 2024-05-04


Column types
types accepts readr’s compact string, with one letter per column:







Letter
Type




c
string


i

float, reading numbers with grouping marks and other characters


l
bool

D

skip the column



types also accepts an array by column name. A value is a Type, a type name such as 'factor', or a letter. The key .default sets the type of every column not named. Here _ffddii_i skips rownames and sex:
$data = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/datasets/main/csv';
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    "{$data}/penguins.csv",
    types: '_ffddii_i',
);
echo $penguins->glimpse(), "\n";

$some = DataFrame::fromCsv(
    "{$data}/penguins.csv",
    types: ['species' => 'factor', '.default' => '_'],
    select: ['species'],
);
echo $some->glimpse();

Columns: 7
$ species           <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adel…
$ island            <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgerse…
$ bill_length_mm    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, …
$ bill_depth_mm     <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, …
$ flipper_length_mm <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186…
$ body_mass_g       <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, …
$ year              <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…
Rows: 344
Columns: 1
$ species <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie…


Guessing
Without explicit types, phibble guesses each column from up to guessMax rows, sampled the way readr 2 samples them. A column is:

bool if every value is T, F, TRUE, FALSE, True, False, true, or false,
int if every value is a whole number (readr guesses double),
float if every value is a number, including Inf and NaN,
date if every value is an ISO 8601 date,
datetime if every value is an ISO 8601 date and time,
time if every value is a time of day as readr reads one: hours of one or two digits, a colon, two digits of minutes, and optionally seconds, a fraction, and AM or PM, such as 7:30, 00:07:15, or 1:30 PM,
string otherwise.

Numbers with leading zeros such as 007 stay strings, as in readr.
As in readr, a time’s minutes and seconds must be under 60, 12 AM is hour 0, PM adds 12 hours to any hour but 12, and a fraction of a second is dropped. The phit extension has no time type, so phibble guesses times in the columns phit reads as text, from the same rows the PHP reader samples.


Parse problems
When a value cannot be parsed as its column’s type, a row has the wrong number of fields, or a quoted field is never closed, phibble still returns the data. The value becomes NA, and the read raises one E_USER_WARNING that lists the problems. Rows are numbered as in readr::problems(): the first data row is row 2, and skipped, blank, and comment lines are not counted.


Quotes
Quoted fields follow readr 2’s rules. A field is quoted when its first character is the quote character. Inside a quoted field, a doubled quote is a literal quote. Any other quote turns quoting off or back on and is dropped, so "x "y" z" reads as x y z, and "x "y",z" reads as x y,z. A quote inside a field that does not start with one is kept as it is. With escapeDouble: false, the quotes inside a quoted field are kept, and only the opening and closing quotes are dropped.
Files written with PHP’s fputcsv() and its default backslash escape contain \" instead of "". readr does not treat the backslash as an escape, and neither does phibble unless escapeBackslash: true is passed.
set_error_handler(function (int $level, string $message): bool {
    echo "Warning: {$message}\n";

    return true;
});

$df = DataFrame::fromCsvString(
    "id,score\n1,2.5\n2,oops\n3\n",
    types: ['score' => 'double'],
);

echo $df;
Warning: One or more parsing issues: row 4: expected 2 columns, got 1; column 'score': 1 value could not be parsed as float.
# A tibble: 3 × 2
     id score
  <int> <dbl>
1     1   2.5
2     2  NA  
3     3  NA

text:
Writing CSV
writeCsv($path) writes a file and toCsv() returns the text. The format follows readr’s write_csv(). Values are quoted only when needed, NA is written as NA, logicals as TRUE and FALSE, dates in ISO 8601, and datetimes in UTC with a Z. Times are written as hms writes a column: one number of fraction digits for the column, and hours padded with spaces to one width. Factors are written as their labels, and list-columns throw.
$df = tribble(
    ['name', 'note', 'score', 'seen'],
    ['Ana', 'likes "quotes"', 1e5, true],
    ['Ben', 'a, b', null, false],
);

echo $df->toCsv();
name,note,score,seen
Ana,"likes ""quotes""",100000,TRUE
Ben,"a, b",NA,FALSE
The options are delimiter, na, append, colNames, quote ('needed', 'all', or 'none'), escape, and eol.

title: Reading and writing data
Reading and writing data
text:
Databases

Query results
DataFrame::fromPdo() runs a query with positional or named bindings and loads the result. PostgreSQL and MySQL report each column’s declared type, and phibble uses it:







Declared type
Column type




Text types, JSON, UUID, TIMETZ, intervals, arrays, and enums
string


BOOLEAN (PostgreSQL)
bool


Integer types and MySQL’s YEAR
int


REAL, DOUBLE PRECISION, FLOAT, and DOUBLE
float


NUMERIC and DECIMAL
float, or int when every value is a whole number


DATE
date


TIMESTAMP, TIMESTAMPTZ, and DATETIME
datetime


TIME
time



A text column stays text, so 'TRUE' and '2024-01-02' in a TEXT column are strings. Only values without a declared type are guessed with the CSV rules. SQLite stores values without a column type, so its results are always guessed, and so are results from other drivers.
NUMERIC and DECIMAL values become doubles, as RPostgres and RMariaDB read them:

A value of up to 15 significant digits, such as a NUMERIC(10,2) price, reads back as the same decimal. Arithmetic on it is floating-point.
A longer value is rounded: 12345678901234567.89 reads as 12345678901234568.0.
A string type keeps the database’s exact decimal text.

$accounts = DataFrame::fromPdo(
    $pdo,
    'SELECT id, balance FROM accounts',
    types: ['balance' => 'string'],
);
Explicit types always take precedence over declared ones. fromQuery(), the Laravel ->toDataFrame() macro, and SqlTable::collect() follow the same rules. This example loads nycflights13’s airports into an in-memory SQLite table and runs a query with two bound values:
$high = DataFrame::fromPdo(
    $pdo,
    'SELECT * FROM airports WHERE tzone = ? AND alt > ? ORDER BY alt DESC',
    ['America/New_York', 2000],
);

echo $high;
# A tibble: 7 × 4
  faa   name                                           alt tzone           
  <chr> <chr>                                        <int> <chr>           
1 BLF   Mercer County Airport                         2857 America/New_York
2 BKW   Raleigh County Memorial Airport               2504 America/New_York
3 LWB   Greenbrier Valley Airport                     2302 America/New_York
4 JST   John Murtha Johnstown-Cambria County Airport  2284 America/New_York
5 2G9   Somerset County Airport                       2275 America/New_York
6 AVL   Asheville Regional Airport                    2165 America/New_York
7 BFD   Bradford Regional Airport                     2143 America/New_York


Query builders
DataFrame::fromQuery() loads a query builder without depending on its library:

A Laravel query builder, Eloquent builder, or relation is read through toSql(), getBindings(), and its connection’s PDO object.
A Doctrine DBAL QueryBuilder is read through getSQL() and getParameters(). Pass a PDO or DBAL connection as the second argument to run the SQL through PDO. Without one, the builder runs the query itself and phibble guesses every column, since DBAL results carry no column types.

To keep a query in the database and run operations there, use a SQL table instead.

text: Phibble\Sql\SqlTable is a table backed by a SQL query, like dbplyr’s tbl(). Methods called with expressions compile to SQL for SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL, and the database runs the query when the rows are needed.

Opening a table







Call
Source




tbl($pdo, 'name'), SqlTable::table()
A table or view.

A query with positional (?) or named (:name) bindings.

A Laravel or Doctrine query builder.

Which calls query the database:

Opening a table reads its column names with a LIMIT 0 query. In SQLite, which declares no column types, it also reads the first 1,000 rows to guess date, datetime, and time columns.
nrow() and count() run a COUNT(*) query, and types() collects the first 1,000 rows.
collect(), toRows(), column(), iteration, and printing load the rows.
Other methods and showQuery() run nothing. showQuery() returns the SQL with ? placeholders, and bindings() returns their values in order.

This example queries an in-memory SQLite table, penguins, loaded from the Palmer penguins data in the PHPstats datasets:
$penguins = tbl($pdo, 'penguins');

$summary = $penguins
    ->filter(col('year')->eq(2008))
    ->groupBy(['species'])
    ->summarize([
        'n' => n(),
        'mass' => mean(col('body_mass_g'), na_rm: true),
    ]);

echo get_class($summary), "\n\n";
echo $summary->showQuery(), "\n\n";
echo json_encode($summary->bindings()), "\n\n";
echo $summary->collect();

title: SQL tables
text:
What compiles to SQL
select(), rename(), filter(), mutate(), arrange(), groupBy(), summarize(), distinct(), slice(), head(), and join() compile when their arguments are expressions or column names. The compiled SQL keeps R’s semantics:

An aggregate returns NA when its group contains NA, unless na_rm: true. phibble adds a check on the count of non-NULL values, since SQL aggregates skip NULL.
Cumulative functions return NA after the first NA.
Ranks leave NA rows unranked.
isIn() never returns NA.
/ returns a float, and division by zero gives NA.
Groups in summarize() output are sorted, with NA last.
Text compares in byte order and case-sensitively, through COLLATE "C" in PostgreSQL and utf8mb4_0900_bin in MySQL.

title: SQL tables
section: When the table falls back to memory
text:
When the table falls back to memory
When an argument has no faithful SQL translation, the SqlTable runs the query so far, collects its rows into PHP, and runs the method in memory. The method returns a DataFrame, so every later step also runs in memory, with DataFrame’s values apart from the known differences. Here mul() compiles, and round() and a closure fall back:
$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:');
$t = tbl($pdo, <<<'SQL'
    SELECT 1 AS id, 2.5 AS x
    UNION ALL SELECT 2, 3.5
    SQL);

$doubled = $t->mutate(['y' => col('x')->mul(2)]);
$rounded = $t->mutate(['y' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x'))]);
$closure = $t->filter(fn ($r) => $r->x > 3);

echo get_class($doubled), "\n";
echo get_class($rounded), "\n";
echo get_class($closure), "\n";

echo $rounded;

PostgreSQL runs FULL JOIN only on merge- or hash-joinable conditions, which NA-matching keys are not.

SQLite column types
SQLite compares by storage class, and it orders all text above all numbers. A column declared without a type stores bound values as text, so col('x')->gt(0) is true for every row of such a column. Declare column types (INTEGER, REAL, TEXT) when creating SQLite tables that phibble will query.

title: SQL tables
text:
Known differences
These cases can differ from DataFrame, because the database cannot represent R’s result:

MySQL has no infinity or NaN. Results that are Inf, -Inf, or NaN in R, such as x / 0, log(0), or mean() of no values, are NA in MySQL. SQLite stores infinities but has no NaN, so NaN is NA there.
Integer arithmetic beyond 64 bits fails in the database, where DataFrame switches to a double.
Joins do not warn about unexpected many-to-many matches.
Column names starting with __phibble_ are reserved for the hidden columns that keep row order and window results.

title: SQL tables
text:
Row order and window functions
SQL tables have no row order of their own. phibble numbers the rows of the source query when the table is opened and keeps that number through every step.

Collected rows follow arrange(), and otherwise the source order. arrange() is stable, so ties keep the source order.
The source order is the order in which the database returns the source query’s rows. A stored table does not fix it, so add arrange() when the order matters.
Rows from a SQL join have no defined order.
Window functions such as lag() and cumsum() use order_by: where given, then the arrange() order, then the source order.
Grouped mutate() and filter() compile to OVER (PARTITION BY ...).

This example totals the precipitation at each airport for June to August 2013, in inches, from a SQLite table of nycflights13’s weather, then takes a running total and each month’s share of the wettest month:
$weather = tbl($pdo, 'weather');

$out = $weather
    ->filter(col('month')->between(6, 8))
    ->groupBy(['origin', 'month'])
    ->summarize(['precip' => sum(col('precip'))])
    ->groupBy(['origin'])
    ->arrange(['origin', 'month'])
    ->mutate([
        'running' => cumsum(col('precip')),
        'of_wettest' => col('precip')
            ->div(max(col('precip'), na_rm: true)),
    ]);

echo $out->showQuery(), "\n\n";
echo $out->collect();
